title: Serplulimab, carboplatin and etoposide
purpose: This treatment aims to control extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, relieve symptoms and help people live longer. The balance of benefit, side effects and daily life is individual; it is generally not offered with an expectation of cure.

agents.name: Serplulimab
agents.explanation: Serplulimab is an antibody that blocks PD-1, a control switch on immune T cells. Some cancers use PD-L1 or PD-L2 to engage this switch and reduce the immune response. Blocking it can help immune cells attack cancer. The same immune activation can inflame healthy organs, so new symptoms need assessment even after treatment stops.
agents.watch: The immune system can also inflame healthy organs. New cough, diarrhoea, unusual weakness, severe headache, thirst or a spreading rash need prompt advice. Effects can start during treatment or after it finishes.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin and hormone glands
Immune effects can also involve the heart, pancreas, nervous system or blood cells
Some hormone effects need lasting replacement treatment; immune effects can begin after the final dose

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin is a platinum-containing chemotherapy. Inside cells, it forms chemical attachments to DNA, including links that stop DNA strands working normally. This disrupts copying and repair and can lead to cell death. Healthy cells can also be injured, especially blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. The kidneys help remove carboplatin, so kidney function is used to calculate the dose. AUC 5 describes a target drug exposure over time; it is not a fixed dose of 5 mg.
agents.watch: Low blood counts, nausea and vomiting can occur. An allergic reaction is also possible: tell the nurse immediately if you feel flushed, itchy, tight-chested or unwell during the drip.
risks: Low blood counts, infection or bleeding

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.alias: Chemotherapy; IV or a separately prescribed capsule alternative
agents.mechanism: Interferes with DNA repair during cell division
agents.explanation: Etoposide blocks topoisomerase II, an enzyme that helps untangle DNA. It can leave DNA breaks unrepaired so that dividing cancer cells die. Healthy dividing cells are affected too, which can lower blood counts, irritate the mouth and bowel and cause hair loss. Kidney function, liver tests and albumin help the team choose a safe dose. Capsules have different dosing instructions from the drip.
agents.watch: Report fever or sudden illness immediately. During a drip, tell the nurse about dizziness, flushing, breathing difficulty or pain at the cannula. If capsules are prescribed, do not take an extra dose after vomiting or a missed dose without advice.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Hair loss and mouth or bowel symptoms
Infusion reactions and low blood pressure
A delayed risk of treatment-related leukaemia

phases.label: Induction · four planned cycles
phases.detail: Induction lasts four planned 21-day cycles unless treatment needs to stop earlier. On Day 1 you receive serplulimab, carboplatin and etoposide by drip. With the standard IV schedule, etoposide is repeated on Days 2 and 3.

phases.label: Maintenance · after induction
phases.detail: After induction, carboplatin and etoposide stop. Serplulimab alone can continue every three weeks while it is helping and its risks remain acceptable. There is no fixed universal number of maintenance cycles in this NCCP regimen.

timeline.label: Blood counts / infection
timeline.text: Counts may fall between visits · timing varies

timeline.label: Immune effects
timeline.text: Any day · also after treatment ends

day_groups.title: Day 1: three medicines during induction
day_groups.body: Serplulimab is given first over about 60 minutes at the first visit. If tolerated, later doses may take about 30 minutes. Carboplatin takes about 30 minutes and IV etoposide about 60 minutes. Assessment, preparation and observation add time. Days 2–3 need further etoposide visits unless the separate oral alternative has been prescribed.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm Days 2–3 etoposide arrangements, your written support prescription and urgent contact number.

day_groups.title: Etoposide Days 2–3 and early recovery
day_groups.body: Your team may instead prescribe etoposide by drip on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2 and 3. This is a separate alternative, not extra treatment. Oral and IV doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Confirm which plan you have; take the capsules on an empty stomach as prescribed. Anti-sickness support must cover the actual treatment days and afterwards. Take only the written plan; ask before adding duplicate medicines.
day_groups.action: Contact the team for persistent vomiting, inability to drink, new diarrhoea or a problem taking prescribed capsules.

day_groups.title: Keep checking how you feel
day_groups.body: Blood counts may be reduced between treatments. You cannot tell your count from the date or from how well you feel. Fatigue or mouth symptoms may affect eating and daily activity.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent advice below for fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell, including with a normal temperature.

day_groups.title: Prepare for your next review
day_groups.body: Some symptoms may settle; others can continue or appear for the first time. Improvement does not prove your blood counts have recovered. The next treatment depends on your review and tests.
day_groups.action: Bring your symptom record and questions. Confirm the next appointment: the next Day 1 is usually 21 days after this cycle's Day 1, if treatment proceeds.

support.title: Induction: plan each treatment day
support.text: Day 1 carboplatin has a stronger anti-sickness plan. Days 2–3 etoposide also need planned cover, with review for two days after the final chemotherapy dose. Ask for one reconciled schedule; do not add another steroid or anti-sickness course yourself.

support.title: Maintenance: a different prescription
support.text: Serplulimab alone usually does not need the routine chemotherapy anti-sickness course. Continue the alert card and immune symptom checks; new nausea or vomiting may need investigation, not just extra anti-sickness tablets.

questions.q: How will we know if it is helping?
questions.a: Ask your oncologist what the treatment is aiming to achieve for you, when scans are planned and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping it. How you feel and the amount of side effects do not reliably show how well treatment is working.

questions.q: Why might a cycle be delayed?
questions.a: A delay can give time to recover or investigate a new symptom. It is a safety decision, not a personal failure. Ask which medicines are affected, what needs to improve and when you will be reviewed.

questions.q: Will I get every side effect?
questions.a: No. The body map shows selected possibilities, not a prediction. Ask about common effects, serious less common effects, and any long-term risks that matter particularly to you. The same symptom can have several causes.

questions.q: What should I organise before starting?
questions.a: Confirm blood-test and Day Ward arrangements, transport home, your medicines schedule and a thermometer. Keep the oncology contact instructions and immunotherapy alert card available. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information if useful.

questions.q: What else belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: Your priorities, expected benefit, alternatives including supportive care, fertility, contraception, pregnancy or breastfeeding, work, driving and the possibility of lasting side effects. You can ask more questions or reconsider treatment at any stage.

questions.q: Do more side effects mean the treatment is working better?
questions.a: No. Side effects are not a reliable personal measure of cancer response. Report them so they can be treated; do not tolerate serious symptoms in the hope that they are a sign of benefit.

questions.q: Do all three medicines continue indefinitely?
questions.a: Induction lasts four planned 21-day cycles unless treatment needs to stop earlier. On Day 1 you receive serplulimab, carboplatin and etoposide by drip. With the standard IV schedule, etoposide is repeated on Days 2 and 3. After induction, carboplatin and etoposide stop. Serplulimab alone can continue every three weeks while it is helping and its risks remain acceptable. There is no fixed universal number of maintenance cycles in this NCCP regimen.

questions.q: What should I say when calling about a symptom?
questions.a: Give the current medicines or say you are in maintenance, the last treatment date, what changed and when, your temperature and whether you can eat, drink and pass urine. Do not delay calling to collect every detail.

Immune effects can arise after the final serplulimab dose. Keep the alert card and urgent contact plan. Follow-up of blood counts, organ changes and scans follows the team’s plan; no universal scan interval is imposed by this regimen.

questions.q: Will I come to hospital on all three treatment days?
questions.a: Usually with the standard IV induction plan, yes. Some people receive a separate capsule prescription for Days 2 and 3. Confirm the route and exact schedule before arranging transport; never substitute capsules for a drip yourself.

questions.q: What if I miss or vomit an etoposide capsule dose?
questions.a: Contact the oncology team or pharmacist for instructions. Do not double the next dose or repeat a vomited dose without advice. Store and handle capsules exactly as the pharmacy advises.

chapters.title: Understanding the treatment aim
chapters.intro: Take one section at a time and discuss what matters to you.

items.title: What do the words mean?
items.text: Small-cell describes the cancer cells seen under the microscope. Extensive-stage means it is too widespread for the limited-stage treatment approach. First-line means the first drug treatment for this stage. This regimen combines two chemotherapy medicines with serplulimab immunotherapy.

items.title: What is treatment trying to achieve?
items.text: The usual aims are cancer control, symptom relief and longer life while considering quality of life. It is generally not given with an expectation of cure. Some people have a prolonged response; others do not. Your team uses your cancer tests, general health and preferences to choose a plan.

items.title: What are the alternatives?
items.text: Ask about other appropriate systemic treatments, a clinical trial and symptom-focused care. Palliative care can support symptoms and daily life while you receive active cancer treatment. This regimen has no required PD-L1 cutoff; that does not guarantee benefit.

items.title: Tell the team your starting point
items.text: Describe usual breathing, bowel pattern, energy, skin and nerve symptoms. Mention autoimmune illness, previous lung inflammation, infection and all medicines including steroids and supplements. Changes are easier to recognise when the team knows what is normal for you.

items.title: Prepare the practical details
items.text: Keep the oncology and out-of-hours numbers, a thermometer and the immunotherapy alert card available. Check blood-test appointments, transport and who can help at home. Ask for written medicine directions and accessible information.

items.title: What happens on the day?
items.text: Serplulimab is given first over about 60 minutes at the first visit. If tolerated, later doses may take about 30 minutes. Carboplatin takes about 30 minutes and IV etoposide about 60 minutes. Assessment, preparation and observation add time. Days 2–3 need further etoposide visits unless the separate oral alternative has been prescribed. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, itching, chest pain, dizziness, breathing changes or pain around the drip.

chapters.title: Etoposide: confirm the route
chapters.intro: There are two NCCP schedules. Your prescription chooses one.

items.title: Standard IV schedule
items.text: Etoposide is given by drip on each of Days 1, 2 and 3 during induction. Serplulimab and carboplatin are given on Day 1. The next cycle is planned 21 days after Day 1, if your team confirms it.

items.title: Separate IV and capsule alternative
items.text: Your team may instead prescribe etoposide by drip on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2 and 3. This is a separate alternative, not extra treatment. Oral and IV doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Confirm which plan you have; take the capsules on an empty stomach as prescribed. Capsules are supplied in different strengths; your label specifies the number to take. Do not open, crush or share capsules. Ask the pharmacist about handling, storage and returning unused doses.

chapters.title: What tests and scans check
chapters.intro: A normal earlier test does not rule out a new problem.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils help fight infection, platelets help stop bleeding, and red cells carry oxygen. Counts can fall between visits. You cannot know a count from the day of the cycle or from feeling well.

items.title: Kidneys, liver and hormones
items.text: Kidney function helps set carboplatin dosing and may affect etoposide dosing. Liver tests and albumin also matter for etoposide. Serplulimab can inflame organs and hormone glands, so blood glucose and thyroid checks continue during maintenance. Report new symptoms even if an earlier test was normal.

items.title: Scans and treatment review
items.text: The team sets the scan schedule and reviews scans with symptoms and examination. Stable cancer can be a worthwhile result. Report new symptoms before the next scan; do not assume worsening is evidence that immune treatment is working.

items.title: Delays and changed doses
items.text: Chemotherapy may be delayed or reduced for toxicity. Serplulimab is held or stopped for relevant toxicity rather than dose-reduced. Ask which medicine is changing and why. Omitted checks are not the same as normal results.

chapters.title: Side effects and what to do
chapters.intro: Selected possibilities are shown; this is not a prediction or a complete medicine leaflet.

items.title: Nausea, vomiting and appetite
items.text: Take prescribed anti-sickness medicines as directed. Small meals and regular sips may help. Report poor control early; persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down or much less urine needs prompt advice.

items.title: Fatigue and weakness
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Sudden severe weakness, dizziness, breathlessness or inability to manage basic tasks needs assessment: infection, anaemia or hormone problems can resemble ordinary tiredness.

items.title: Mouth and bowels
items.text: Use gentle mouth care and report painful ulcers or difficulty drinking. Report new diarrhoea, abdominal pain or blood in stools promptly because immune bowel inflammation is possible. Ask about constipation from anti-sickness drugs or pain medicines; severe pain, swelling or vomiting needs assessment.

items.title: Hair, skin, hearing and nerves
items.text: Chemotherapy can cause hair loss. Report new hearing changes, numbness or weakness, and tell the team if these affect balance or daily tasks. Serplulimab can cause immune skin reactions: blistering, peeling or sores around the eyes or mouth need urgent advice.

items.title: Bruising and bleeding
items.text: Report unusual bruising, nosebleeds or bleeding gums. Heavy bleeding, black stools with weakness or severe breathlessness needs urgent assessment. Do not change prescribed blood thinners without advice.

chapters.title: Serplulimab: symptoms that deserve special attention
chapters.intro: Immune treatment can cause inflammation in healthy organs, during treatment or after it ends. Keep your immunotherapy alert card and tell other healthcare professionals you have received serplulimab.

items.title: Lungs, bowel, liver and kidneys
items.text: New cough or breathlessness, diarrhoea, yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, reduced urine or swelling can signal inflammation. These symptoms also have other causes, including infection and cancer. Contact the team promptly for assessment rather than trying to identify the organ or diagnosis yourself.

items.title: Hormones, heart and nervous system
items.text: Report unusual weakness, persistent headache, dizziness, marked thirst, frequent urination, palpitations, muscle weakness or changes in vision. Severe chest pain, collapse, confusion, seizures or major breathing difficulty require emergency care. Some hormone effects need ongoing replacement treatment even after immunotherapy stops.

items.title: Why early reporting matters
items.text: The team may pause treatment and investigate. Some reactions need steroids or other immune-suppressing treatment; others need hormone replacement. These are different from the short planned steroid course around chemotherapy. Do not start leftover steroids, change their dose or stop a prescribed course yourself. Carry the treatment name when attending emergency care.

items.title: Muscle weakness and vision changes
items.text: New muscle weakness, tiring much more easily, drooping eyelids, swallowing difficulty or new visual symptoms need urgent advice. Difficulty breathing or swallowing needs emergency care. Serplulimab can cause serious nerve-muscle or eye inflammation; do not wait for the next appointment.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: The aim is a plan that fits your life as well as your treatment. Bring practical concerns to the team early.

items.title: Food, fluids and weight
items.text: Aim for enough food and fluid to maintain strength, using foods you tolerate. Tell the team about weight loss, swallowing problems or difficulty shopping or cooking; ask for dietitian support. A fixed fluid target is not right for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney disease. “Anti-cancer” diets, fasting and high-dose supplements are not substitutes for treatment and can create nutritional or interaction problems.

items.title: Movement, work and rest
items.text: Try activity that feels manageable and increase or reduce it according to symptoms. Short walks or simple daily tasks may be more realistic than your usual exercise. Discuss work adjustments and travel plans. Do not drive if dizzy, unusually tired or affected by sedating medicines. Sudden deterioration should prompt assessment, not an attempt to push through exercise.

items.title: Infection precautions without isolation
items.text: Wash hands, practise food hygiene and avoid close contact with people who are unwell. Ask about vaccinations and their timing; some vaccines are unsuitable during treatment. You can usually still spend time with family. Keep your urgent contact plan available: precautions reduce risk but do not make fever or sudden illness safe to watch at home.

items.title: Intimacy, fertility and pregnancy
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before starting if relevant. Do not become pregnant or breastfeed during this treatment. NCCP specifies effective contraception during serplulimab and for at least six months after the last dose for women of childbearing potential; the team must reconcile all medicines into one written contraception and breastfeeding plan. Report a possible pregnancy promptly.

items.title: Emotional support and choices
items.text: It is reasonable to feel worried, angry, uncertain or overloaded. Ask for psycho-oncology, counselling, social work or family support. You can request information in smaller pieces, an interpreter or a written summary. Tell the team what you most want to preserve in daily life. You can revisit treatment decisions and ask for more time or another explanation.

chapters.title: A short treatment dictionary
chapters.intro: Terms you may hear in clinic.

items.title: Cycle · induction · maintenance
items.text: A cycle is a planned treatment-and-interval period. Induction is the initial combination phase. Maintenance is ongoing treatment after that phase; it does not mean side-effect-free treatment.

items.title: Response · stable disease · progression
items.text: Response means the cancer has reduced by the assessment used. Stable disease means it has not changed enough to meet response or progression criteria. Progression means growth or spread meeting the assessment criteria. Your team interprets these alongside how you are feeling.

items.title: Neutropenia · anaemia · thrombocytopenia
items.text: Neutropenia means low infection-fighting neutrophils. Anaemia means low haemoglobin. Thrombocytopenia means low platelets. These are different results with different implications; one normal number does not establish that all treatment risks are low.

items.title: Immune-related · colitis · pneumonitis
items.text: Immune-related effects come from immune activity against healthy tissue. Colitis means inflammation of the colon; pneumonitis means inflammation in the lungs. A symptom alone cannot establish either diagnosis.

evidence.title: Why this treatment is offered
evidence.intro: A randomised study found that adding serplulimab to carboplatin and etoposide helped people with previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer live longer than chemotherapy alone.
evidence.interpretation: These results describe groups. They cannot predict your own response or length of life. Ask what benefit is realistic for you and what matters most in your daily life.
evidence.population: Adults with previously untreated extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer in ASTRUM-005.
evidence.limitations: The trial studied selected people with performance status 0–1 and IV etoposide. The NCCP regimen permits performance status 0–2 and an oral alternative, so the trial is not a separate result for every NCCP-eligible person or for the oral schedule.

indication_text: For adults starting drug treatment for extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer. This regimen does not require a minimum PD-L1 result.
schedule_summary: Induction lasts four planned 21-day cycles unless treatment needs to stop earlier. On Day 1 you receive serplulimab, carboplatin and etoposide by drip. With the standard IV schedule, etoposide is repeated on Days 2 and 3. After induction, carboplatin and etoposide stop. Serplulimab alone can continue every three weeks while it is helping and its risks remain acceptable. There is no fixed universal number of maintenance cycles in this NCCP regimen. Your team may instead prescribe etoposide by drip on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2 and 3. This is a separate alternative, not extra treatment. Oral and IV doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Confirm which plan you have; take the capsules on an empty stomach as prescribed.
administration_text: Serplulimab is given first over about 60 minutes at the first visit. If tolerated, later doses may take about 30 minutes. Carboplatin takes about 30 minutes and IV etoposide about 60 minutes. Assessment, preparation and observation add time. Days 2–3 need further etoposide visits unless the separate oral alternative has been prescribed.
monitoring_summary: Blood counts, kidney and liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle. Thyroid tests are repeated every 3–6 weeks. The medicine information also recommends pancreatic enzyme checks at baseline and periodically. Other tests and scans depend on symptoms and the consultant plan.

monitoring_schedule.note: Relative stages, not equally spaced dates. No patient dates are needed. Pancreatic enzyme checks supplement NCCP from the current product information; the team confirms timing and reviews every result.

urgent_extra: Contact oncology immediately for temperature 37.5°C or above, 36°C or below, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell, even with a normal temperature. New cough, diarrhoea, severe weakness, marked thirst, reduced urine or blistering skin need prompt assessment. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, seizures or major bleeding need emergency help. Keep the immunotherapy alert card after treatment.
consent_support: Discuss expected benefit, alternatives including symptom-focused care, infection and bleeding risks, immune organ inflammation and possible lasting hormone replacement, infusion reactions, fertility/contraception, delayed effects and the different IV/oral etoposide schedules. Your priorities and the option to reconsider treatment belong in this conversation.

sections.title: Appointments
sections.text: Serplulimab is given first over about 60 minutes at the first visit. If tolerated, later doses may take about 30 minutes. Carboplatin takes about 30 minutes and IV etoposide about 60 minutes. Assessment, preparation and observation add time. Days 2–3 need further etoposide visits unless the separate oral alternative has been prescribed.

sections.title: Route and phases
sections.text: Induction lasts four planned 21-day cycles unless treatment needs to stop earlier. On Day 1 you receive serplulimab, carboplatin and etoposide by drip. With the standard IV schedule, etoposide is repeated on Days 2 and 3. Your team may instead prescribe etoposide by drip on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2 and 3. This is a separate alternative, not extra treatment. Oral and IV doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Confirm which plan you have; take the capsules on an empty stomach as prescribed.

sections.title: Maintenance visits
sections.text: After induction, carboplatin and etoposide stop. Serplulimab alone can continue every three weeks while it is helping and its risks remain acceptable. There is no fixed universal number of maintenance cycles in this NCCP regimen.

sections.title: Medicines and urgent advice
sections.text: Keep the written anti-sickness schedule, capsule instructions if relevant, thermometer, immunotherapy alert card and oncology numbers available. Ask early about transport or help at home.

anatomy: Severe weakness, headache, dizziness, thirst, confusion or seizures need prompt or emergency assessment.
New cough or breathlessness: contact the team; severe breathing difficulty needs emergency help.
Chest pain, racing heart or collapse need urgent assessment.
Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or new severe nausea need advice; tests can detect changes before symptoms.
Much less urine, swelling or persistent vomiting need advice; kidney function affects doses.
New diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, blood in stool or inability to drink need prompt assessment.
Blisters, peeling, mouth or eye sores, new weakness or numbness need advice.
Fever, shivering or sudden illness: call oncology immediately. Report unusual bleeding or bruising.

chronology_notes.text: Your team may instead prescribe etoposide by drip on Day 1 and capsules twice daily on Days 2 and 3. This is a separate alternative, not extra treatment.
